  in seconds: windows named, panes split, and commands started. Copy mode lets you scroll back, search, and copy text
  from output without touching the mouse. Plugins add things like saving sessions across reboots and showing status
  information.

  Multiplexers have critics. Modern terminal emulators already have tabs and splits, and tiling window managers can
  arrange terminals well. Nested prefix keys, odd behavior with color and clipboard support, and a real learning curve
  all add friction. On a local machine, a multiplexer can be more than you need.

  Still, none of those alternatives keeps your work alive on a remote server after the connection drops. As long as
  people work on machines they reach over a network, terminal multiplexers will keep their place. What began as a fix
  for unreliable phone lines now shapes how many developers work at the command line.
